patient.name: Kwame Mensah
patient.setting: Acute Medical Unit, day 2 of admission
patient.complaint: Admitted with pneumonia and sepsis; now oozing from his cannula sites and gums
background: Retired bus driver from Brixton; ex-smoker
No previous bleeding problems; not on anticoagulants
Started IV co-amoxiclav and clarithromycin yesterday

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with a septic, obstetric, trauma or cancer patient who suddenly bleeds from several sites with a petechial rash. The distractors are TTP, ITP and liver failure.

points: Kwame, 66, admitted yesterday with **pneumonia and sepsis**.
Overnight: **oozing from both cannula sites** and his gums.
His catheter bag has turned pink (**haematuria**).
He is more breathless and drowsy.

visual.title: Kwame's admission chest X-ray
visual.caption: Right lower zone consolidation: the **pneumonia** that set off his sepsis.

steps.text: The trigger is in his chest: severe sepsis from pneumonia.

steps.lead: Kwame's sepsis has switched on clotting **everywhere at once**: tiny clots use up his platelets and factors, so now he bleeds.
**Sepsis** is the most important trigger, and that is Kwame's. Always ask: is this patient septic, pregnant, injured or known to have cancer?

points: **Petechiae and purpura** across his legs and trunk.
Large bruise around an old blood-test site.

steps.lead: Bleeding from **several sites**, a petechial rash, shock and failing organs: Kwame has the full picture. His film will show schistocytes.

steps.q: Kwame is septic and bleeding from several sites with a petechial rash. Which is most likely?
steps.r: A septic patient bleeding from multiple sites is **DIC**. ITP and TTP have normal clotting times; haemophilia is lifelong.

steps.title: Low platelets and bleeding: which one?
head: Feature
DIC
TTP
ITP
Liver failure

steps.text: Schistocytes appear in **both DIC and TTP**. The clotting decides: prolonged PT and APTT with **low fibrinogen** means DIC; TTP clotting is normal.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?' (coagulation screen) or 'Which is the most likely finding on blood film?' (schistocytes). Know the full DIC pattern.

steps.lead: Kwame's **FBC** shows his platelets have crashed, and the **blood film** is checked for schistocytes.

steps.title: Kwame's bloods, day 2
steps.text: Low platelets and fibrinogen, prolonged PT and APTT, very high D-dimer, schistocytes: textbook **DIC**.

steps.lead: Kwame's **coagulation screen** confirms it: every part of the DIC pattern is there.

visual.title: Fibrinogen
visual.label: Kwame 0.8
visual.caption: Fibrinogen is used up making clots. Below **1.5 g/L** in a bleeding patient means cryoprecipitate.

steps.q: Which result best separates Kwame's DIC from TTP?
steps.r: **Low fibrinogen** (with prolonged PT/APTT) means clotting factors are being consumed: DIC. The other three occur in TTP too.

steps.title: The DIC blood pattern
steps.caption: Everything that is used up falls; the breakdown product (D-dimer) rises.

steps.text: Repeat the coagulation screen: DIC is **dynamic**. A falling platelet count and fibrinogen over hours matters more than a single value.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?': **treat the cause** (antibiotics, delivery, treat the cancer). If actively bleeding, add platelets, FFP and cryoprecipitate.

steps.lead: Kwame's DIC will only switch off when the **sepsis** is controlled: his antibiotics are reviewed with microbiology and cultures chased.

steps.q: Kwame is oozing from several sites. Platelets 34, fibrinogen 0.8. What is needed for his bleeding?
steps.r: Active bleeding in DIC needs the consumed parts replaced: **platelets, FFP and cryoprecipitate** (for fibrinogen).

steps.lead: Kwame is **actively bleeding**, so he gets platelets, FFP and cryoprecipitate for his fibrinogen of 0.8.

steps.title: Managing DIC
nodes: Sepsis → antibiotics; obstetric → deliver; cancer → treat it
Not bleeding → do not transfuse just for the numbers
Support: IV fluids, organ monitoring, repeat clotting
steps.caption: Blood products buy time; treating the cause is the cure.

steps.lead: Kwame moves to HDU for **IV fluids**, organ support and repeated coagulation profiles.

visual.title: Kwame recovers as the sepsis is treated
visual.caption: Once the infection is controlled, platelets climb and the PT normalises. Products alone would not have done this.

steps.lead: Kwame's care follows the **BSH DIC guideline**: treat the cause, and give products for bleeding rather than for lab numbers alone.

steps.text: **Tranexamic acid** is generally avoided in DIC: blocking fibrinolysis when clots are forming everywhere can worsen thrombosis.

science.exam: Expect applied mechanism questions: why DIC causes bleeding and clotting together, why schistocytes form, and why the D-dimer is high.

steps.lead: Kwame's bacteria trigger **tissue factor** release, which fires the coagulation cascade throughout his small vessels.
Kwame clots in his microcirculation yet bleeds from his gums: his platelets and factors are being **used faster than he can make them**.
Kwame's red cells are **sliced by fibrin strands** in partly blocked vessels, giving schistocytes: a microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia.
Kwame's D-dimer of 8400 shows his body is **breaking down** the clots; his low fibrinogen shows it is being used up making them.

steps.q: Why is Kwame's D-dimer so high?
steps.r: D-dimer is a **fibrin breakdown product**: it rises because fibrinolysis is breaking down the widespread clots.

steps.text: Think of DIC as **consumption**: whatever clotting uses up falls (platelets, fibrinogen, factors), whatever it produces rises (D-dimer).

mcq.q: What is the most important trigger of DIC?
mcq.r: **Sepsis** is the most important trigger; the others are recognised causes.

mcq.q: Which presentation is typical of DIC?
o: Bleeding from multiple sites with petechiae
mcq.r: **Bleeding from multiple sites**, petechiae, purpura, shock and organ dysfunction.

mcq.q: Which blood film finding is characteristic of DIC?
Which is the gold-standard test for DIC?
mcq.r: The **coagulation screen** (PT, APTT, fibrinogen, D-dimer) with platelets.

o: Low fibrinogen, high D-dimer, prolonged PT and APTT
Low platelets with normal PT and APTT
mcq.r: **Low fibrinogen, low platelets, high D-dimer, prolonged PT and APTT.**

mcq.q: What is the first-line treatment of DIC?
mcq.r: **Treat the cause**: antibiotics for sepsis, delivery for obstetric causes, treat the cancer.

mcq.q: Which blood product replaces fibrinogen in a bleeding DIC patient?
Which blood products are given for active bleeding in DIC?
Why does DIC cause bleeding and clotting at the same time?
o: Factors are consumed faster than replaced
mcq.r: Widespread clotting **consumes** platelets and factors faster than they can be replaced.

mcq.q: Which molecule starts the clotting cascade in DIC from sepsis?

technique.stem: A 71 year old woman is in the intensive care unit with septic shock from a perforated bowel. On day 2 she starts bleeding from her line sites and wound, and has a petechial rash. Her temperature is 38.6°C, pulse rate 118 bpm and BP 86/50 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis question about bleeding in a sick patient: read the clotting.

clues: bleeding from her line sites and wound
steps.x: Sepsis trigger, bleeding from several sites. Low platelets and fibrinogen, prolonged PT/APTT, high D-dimer.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **DIC** triggered by sepsis.

elim: Haemophilia A is inherited, with an isolated prolonged APTT and normal platelets.
ITP has low platelets with normal clotting and fibrinogen.
TTP has normal PT, APTT and fibrinogen.
Vitamin K deficiency prolongs PT but does not drop platelets or fibrinogen.

steps.x: **A. DIC.** Rule: septic + bleeding everywhere + everything consumed = DIC.

technique.stem: A 58 year old man with pneumonia and sepsis develops petechiae and bleeding gums. His temperature is 38.4°C, pulse rate 112 bpm and BP 92/58 mmHg. His platelet count is 38 ×10⁹/L and the blood film shows schistocytes. The team must decide between DIC and thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura.
technique.q: Which result would best support DIC rather than TTP?

steps.x: Which result separates DIC from TTP.

clues: between DIC and thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura
steps.x: Both cause low platelets and schistocytes. You need the clotting factor result.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Low fibrinogen** (and prolonged PT/APTT): factors are consumed in DIC, not in TTP.

elim: High LDH reflects haemolysis in both.
Anaemia occurs in both.
Low platelets occur in both.
Schistocytes occur in both.

steps.x: **B.** Rule: clotting factors decide; DIC consumes fibrinogen, TTP does not.

technique.stem: A 64 year old man with E. coli bacteraemia from a urinary source is on intravenous antibiotics. He is now oozing from cannula sites and has haematuria. His pulse rate is 108 bpm and BP 98/60 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate next step to manage his bleeding?
o: Platelets, fresh frozen plasma and cryoprecipitate

steps.x: Management of active bleeding; the cause is already being treated.
Septic DIC with **active bleeding**: platelets 29, fibrinogen 0.7.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Replace what has been consumed: **platelets, FFP and cryoprecipitate**.

elim: Desmopressin is for von Willebrand disease or mild haemophilia A.
Tranexamic acid is generally avoided in DIC; it can worsen thrombosis.
Vitamin K does not replace platelets or fibrinogen.
Protamine reverses heparin; he is not on heparin.

steps.x: **D.** Rule: treat the cause; if bleeding, give platelets, FFP and cryo.

technique.stem: A 33 year old woman has a major placental abruption at 35 weeks. She develops widespread microvascular thrombi but also bleeds from her drip sites and gums. Her platelets and fibrinogen are very low and her D-dimer is very high.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism for her bleeding?
o: Consumption of platelets and clotting factors by widespread clotting
Impaired hepatic synthesis of clotting factors

steps.x: A mechanism question: why she clots and bleeds together.

clues: bleeds from her drip sites and gums
platelets and fibrinogen are very low
steps.x: An obstetric trigger releases tissue factor; clots everywhere, then bleeding.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Consumption**: platelets and factors used up faster than replaced.

elim: Antibody destruction is ITP, with normal clotting.
Factor VIII deficiency is haemophilia A, inherited.
Nothing suggests liver failure; the D-dimer is very high.
She is not on warfarin and fibrinogen would be normal.

steps.x: **B.** Rule: DIC = consumptive coagulopathy.

practice.stem: A 69 year old man is admitted with a severe chest infection. On day 3 he develops bruising, bleeding from his gums and blood in his urine. His temperature is 38.7°C, pulse rate 120 bpm and BP 82/46 mmHg. He has a petechial rash on his legs. He is not jaundiced.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Sepsis with bleeding from multiple sites, low platelets and fibrinogen and prolonged PT/APTT is DIC. TTP, HUS and ITP have normal clotting; normal bilirubin argues against liver failure.

steps.x: Diagnosis in a septic, bleeding patient.

clues: bruising, bleeding from his gums and blood in his urine
steps.x: Sepsis, shock, bleeding from several sites, consumption pattern.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Liver failure brings jaundice; bilirubin is normal.
HUS follows bloody diarrhoea with AKI and normal clotting.
ITP has normal clotting and he is unwell.
TTP has normal PT, APTT and fibrinogen.

steps.x: **B.** Rule: prolonged clotting + low fibrinogen + low platelets in sepsis = DIC.

practice.stem: A 31 year old woman at 37 weeks of pregnancy has sudden severe abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding from a placental abruption. She then oozes from her cannula sites. Her pulse rate is 128 bpm and BP 84/52 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of her bleeding from the cannula sites?
practice.e: Placental abruption is a classic obstetric trigger of DIC; low platelets and fibrinogen, prolonged PT and very high D-dimer confirm it.

steps.x: Cause of new bleeding in an obstetric emergency.
Obstetric trigger; consumption pattern. Fibrinogen should be high in pregnancy, so 0.9 is very low.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Gestational thrombocytopenia is mild, with normal clotting.
ITP has normal PT and fibrinogen.
Carriers do not suddenly develop low fibrinogen and platelets.
Von Willebrand disease is lifelong, with normal fibrinogen.

steps.x: **A.** Rule: abruption + oozing = DIC.

practice.stem: A 60 year old man with septic shock develops bleeding from multiple sites. His platelets are 32 ×10⁹/L, PT and APTT are prolonged and fibrinogen is low. His haemoglobin has fallen from 132 to 96 g/L. A blood film is examined.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on the blood film?
practice.e: In DIC, microthrombi fragment red cells into schistocytes (microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia). Howell-Jolly bodies suggest hyposplenism.

steps.x: Most likely blood film finding in DIC.
DIC with a falling haemoglobin: red cells are being sheared.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Schistocytes**.

elim: Bite cells are oxidative haemolysis, e.g. G6PD deficiency.
Howell-Jolly bodies mean hyposplenism.
Spherocytes suggest hereditary spherocytosis or autoimmune haemolysis.
Target cells suggest liver disease or thalassaemia.

steps.x: **C.** Rule: DIC film = schistocytes.

practice.stem: A 19 year old student has a 12 hour history of fever and headache and now has a spreading non-blanching purpuric rash. He is bleeding from his gums. His temperature is 39.4°C, pulse rate 134 bpm and BP 78/40 mmHg. Clotting tests show low platelets, low fibrinogen and a very high D-dimer.
practice.q: Which is the most likely trigger of his coagulopathy?
practice.e: Fever, headache, purpuric rash and shock point to meningococcal sepsis, the commonest trigger of DIC.

steps.x: Asks for the trigger of DIC.

clues: low platelets, low fibrinogen and a very high D-dimer
steps.x: Meningococcal-type sepsis with DIC.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Sepsis**.

elim: APL causes DIC but would not give fever, headache and shock over 12 hours.
No injury in the history.
A 19 year old with a 12 hour illness: not metastatic cancer.
No snake bite.

steps.x: **D.** Rule: sepsis is the most important trigger of DIC.

practice.stem: A 45 year old woman is in intensive care after a major road traffic collision with multiple fractures. On day 1 she starts to ooze from her wounds and line sites. DIC is suspected and a coagulation screen is sent.
practice.q: Which is the most likely set of results?
o: Isolated low platelets with normal clotting
Low fibrinogen, low platelets, high D-dimer, prolonged PT and APTT
Normal platelets with prolonged PT only
practice.e: DIC consumes platelets and fibrinogen, prolongs PT and APTT and raises D-dimer. Isolated low platelets is ITP; isolated prolonged APTT suggests haemophilia.

steps.x: Most likely clotting pattern in DIC.

clues: ooze from her wounds and line sites
steps.x: Trauma is a recognised trigger.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Everything consumed falls, D-dimer rises, clotting times prolong.

elim: Normal clotting with low platelets is ITP.
Isolated prolonged APTT suggests haemophilia or heparin.
Isolated prolonged PT suggests warfarin or vitamin K deficiency.
A reactive thrombocytosis with normal clotting is not DIC.

steps.x: **C.** Rule: DIC pattern = low fibrinogen, low platelets, high D-dimer, long PT and APTT.

practice.stem: A 74 year old man with metastatic prostate cancer has 1 week of easy bruising and nosebleeds, and now oozes from a blood test site. He has no fever and no neurological symptoms. His pulse rate is 94 bpm and BP 128/76 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Malignancy is a recognised trigger of DIC, which can be more gradual in cancer. Low fibrinogen and platelets with prolonged clotting and high D-dimer fit; normal bilirubin and albumin argue against liver failure.

steps.x: Diagnosis of a bleeding tendency in cancer.

clues: oozes from a blood test site
steps.x: Cancer trigger plus the consumption pattern; liver tests normal.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **DIC** from malignancy.

elim: Bilirubin and albumin are normal.
ITP has normal PT, APTT and fibrinogen.
TTP has normal clotting, often with neurological signs.
Vitamin K deficiency does not lower platelets or fibrinogen, or raise D-dimer.

steps.x: **B.** Rule: cancer can trigger DIC; check fibrinogen and D-dimer.

practice.stem: A 67 year old woman with biliary sepsis develops bleeding from her cannula sites and a petechial rash. Her temperature is 38.5°C, pulse rate 116 bpm and BP 90/56 mmHg. Her platelet count is 44 ×10⁹/L.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
practice.e: A coagulation screen (PT, APTT, fibrinogen, D-dimer) is the gold standard for DIC. Blood cultures find the trigger but do not confirm DIC.

steps.x: Confirming DIC, not finding the source.
Septic, bleeding, low platelets: suspect DIC.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Coagulation screen**.

elim: Cultures identify the organism, not the coagulopathy.
Marrow biopsy is not needed for DIC.
DAT tests for autoimmune haemolysis.
LFTs assess the liver, not consumption.

steps.x: **C.** Rule: DIC is confirmed on the coagulation screen.

practice.stem: A 55 year old man with septic shock has bruising and a falling haemoglobin. His PT and APTT are prolonged, fibrinogen is low and D-dimer is high. The haematologist wants to look for evidence of red cell fragmentation.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
practice.e: A blood film (with the FBC) shows schistocytes, the fragmented red cells of DIC. Haptoglobin and reticulocytes show haemolysis but not fragmentation.

steps.x: Which test shows red cell fragments.
DIC with haemolysis; you want to see schistocytes.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Blood film**.

elim: DAT detects antibody-coated red cells.
Electrophoresis is for haemoglobinopathies.
Reticulocytes show marrow response, not fragments.
Low haptoglobin shows haemolysis but not its cause.

steps.x: **A.** Rule: FBC and blood film look for schistocytes.

practice.stem: A 72 year old woman with pyelonephritis and sepsis is found to have DIC on routine bloods. She is not bleeding. Her temperature is 38.8°C, pulse rate 110 bpm and BP 100/62 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
practice.e: First-line DIC management is treating the cause: IV antibiotics for sepsis. She is not bleeding, so products are not given for the numbers alone.

steps.x: Initial management of DIC without bleeding.
Sepsis is the trigger; no active bleeding.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Treat the cause: **IV antibiotics**.

elim: FFP is for active bleeding, not lab values alone.
Tranexamic acid can worsen thrombosis in DIC.
Platelets are for bleeding or very low counts with procedures.
Vitamin K does not reverse consumption.

steps.x: **B.** Rule: DIC first-line = treat the underlying cause.

practice.stem: A 40 year old man with septic DIC is bleeding heavily from a central line site despite platelets and fresh frozen plasma. His pulse rate is 118 bpm and BP 94/58 mmHg. His fibrinogen is 0.6 g/L (1.5–4.0).
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate blood product to give next?
practice.e: Cryoprecipitate is the concentrated source of fibrinogen, used in bleeding DIC with low fibrinogen.

steps.x: Which product next, after platelets and FFP.

clues: despite platelets and fresh frozen plasma
steps.x: Fibrinogen is the missing piece.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Cryoprecipitate** for fibrinogen replacement.

elim: Albumin does not help clotting.
Red cells treat anaemia, not the coagulopathy.
He has already had platelets; fibrinogen is the gap.
PCC lacks fibrinogen and is used to reverse warfarin.

steps.x: **A.** Rule: low fibrinogen in bleeding DIC = cryoprecipitate.

practice.stem: A 34 year old woman at 38 weeks of pregnancy has a placental abruption with fetal distress. She is oozing from her cannula sites. Her pulse rate is 124 bpm and BP 90/54 mmHg. Platelets are 56 ×10⁹/L and fibrinogen is low. Blood products have been requested.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?
practice.e: In obstetric DIC the trigger is the placenta, so delivery treats the cause. Blood products support her until then.

steps.x: Definitive management: remove the trigger.
Obstetric DIC; supportive care already under way.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Deliver the fetus**.

elim: No infection is described.
Heparin would worsen active bleeding.
Magnesium is for eclampsia.
Steroids do not treat DIC.

steps.x: **E.** Rule: obstetric DIC = deliver; septic DIC = antibiotics.

practice.stem: A 62 year old man with septic DIC has a falling haemoglobin, a raised LDH and a low haptoglobin. His blood film shows fragmented red cells. His direct antiglobulin test is negative.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his anaemia?
practice.e: Microthrombi partly block small vessels and shear red cells into schistocytes: a microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia. A negative DAT excludes autoimmune haemolysis.

steps.x: A mechanism question: why the red cells break.
Haemolysis with schistocytes, not antibody-mediated.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Mechanical fragmentation by microthrombi** (MAHA).

elim: The DAT is negative.
Polymerisation is sickle cell disease.
Oxidative damage is G6PD deficiency, with bite cells.
Membrane defects are hereditary spherocytosis.

steps.x: **C.** Rule: schistocytes = red cells cut by microthrombi.

prompts.q: What is DIC, and why does it cause both clotting and bleeding?

points.p: Platelets and clotting factors consumed, causing bleeding

prompts.q: What are the triggers of DIC?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the stem nearly always shows you the trigger.

points.p: Malignancy: metastatic cancer or haematological malignancy
points.why: Acute promyelocytic leukaemia is a classic.

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: bleeding from several sites at once in a sick patient.

points.p: Bleeding from multiple sites: gums, cannula sites, haematuria
points.why: More than one site is the clue.

prompts.q: How do you tell DIC from TTP and ITP?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: look at the clotting times and fibrinogen.

points.p: DIC: prolonged PT and APTT with low fibrinogen
ITP: isolated low platelets, normal film and clotting

prompts.q: Which tests confirm DIC, and what pattern do they show?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: name all five parts.

points.p: Coagulation screen is the gold standard

prompts.q: What is the first-line test and what does the film show?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the 'most likely film finding' is schistocytes.

points.why: Also seen in TTP and HUS.

prompts.q: What is the first-line management of DIC, by trigger?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the cure is treating the cause.

prompts.q: What do you give a patient with DIC who is actively bleeding, and what supportive care?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: cryoprecipitate is for fibrinogen.

points.p: Supportive: IV fluids, monitor organs and coagulation

prompts.q: What sets off DIC, and why are schistocytes seen?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: tissue factor starts it; microthrombi shred red cells.

points.p: Tissue factor release activates the coagulation cascade
points.why: From sepsis, trauma, cancer or obstetric events.

points.p: Microthrombi mechanically fragment red cells in partly blocked vessels

prompts.q: Why is the D-dimer high and the fibrinogen low in DIC?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: one is made into clot, the other is clot broken down.

points.p: D-dimer reflects increased fibrinolysis of fibrin clots
Factors consumed faster than replaced: no reserve for haemostasis

glossary.DIC: Disseminated intravascular coagulation: widespread clotting that uses up platelets and factors, causing bleeding.
glossary.disseminated intravascular coagulation: Widespread activation of clotting in small vessels, consuming platelets and clotting factors and causing bleeding.
glossary.coagulation: The process of blood clotting through the clotting factor cascade.
glossary.microthrombi: Tiny clots in small blood vessels that block flow and damage organs.
glossary.consumptive coagulopathy: Bleeding disorder caused by using up platelets and clotting factors faster than they are made.
glossary.tissue factor: Protein that starts the extrinsic clotting pathway when exposed to blood.
glossary.fibrinogen: Clotting protein converted to fibrin to form clots; low in DIC.
glossary.fibrin: Insoluble protein strands that form the mesh of a blood clot.
glossary.fibrinolysis: Breakdown of fibrin clots by plasmin.
glossary.D-dimer: A breakdown product of fibrin clots; high when clots are forming and being broken down.
glossary.PT: Prothrombin time: tests the extrinsic and common clotting pathways; prolonged in DIC.
glossary.APTT: Activated partial thromboplastin time: tests the intrinsic and common pathways; prolonged in DIC.
glossary.coagulation screen: Blood clotting tests: PT, APTT, fibrinogen and often D-dimer.
glossary.schistocytes: Fragmented red blood cells sheared in damaged small vessels.
glossary.microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia: Red cell destruction as cells are cut by clots in small vessels, giving schistocytes.
glossary.MAHA: Microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia: red cells sheared by microthrombi.
glossary.petechiae: Pinpoint red or purple spots from bleeding into the skin; do not blanch.
glossary.petechial rash: A rash of tiny non-blanching red spots, typical of low platelets.
glossary.purpura: Larger purple patches of bleeding under the skin that do not blanch.
glossary.FFP: Fresh frozen plasma: replaces all the clotting factors.
glossary.fresh frozen plasma: Plasma frozen soon after donation, containing all clotting factors.
glossary.cryoprecipitate: A concentrated blood product rich in fibrinogen, factor VIII and von Willebrand factor.
glossary.platelets: Small cell fragments that plug damaged vessels; also a transfused blood product.
glossary.TTP: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura: platelet clots from ADAMTS13 deficiency with normal clotting times.
glossary.ITP: Immune thrombocytopenia: antibodies destroy platelets; clotting times are normal.
glossary.HUS: Haemolytic uraemic syndrome: haemolysis, low platelets and AKI, often after E. coli O157 diarrhoea.
glossary.placental abruption: Separation of the placenta from the uterus before delivery; a classic obstetric DIC trigger.
glossary.acute promyelocytic leukaemia: A subtype of acute myeloid leukaemia classically complicated by DIC.
glossary.sepsis: Life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated response to infection.
glossary.septic shock: Sepsis with low blood pressure needing vasopressors and a raised lactate despite fluids.
glossary.LDH: Lactate dehydrogenase: an enzyme released when cells, including red cells, break down.
glossary.haptoglobin: Protein that binds free haemoglobin; falls in haemolysis.
glossary.direct antiglobulin test: Coombs test: detects antibodies on red cells in autoimmune haemolysis.
glossary.DAT: Direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test: positive in antibody-mediated haemolysis.
glossary.tranexamic acid: Drug that blocks fibrinolysis; generally avoided in DIC.
glossary.BSH: British Society for Haematology: publishes UK haematology guidelines.
glossary.HDU: High dependency unit: closer monitoring and support than a general ward.
